items.question: How do you understand the apparent performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers through your work on “A ConvNet for the 2020s”?
items.object: The performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers
items.answer: So that was a really interesting story. We were working on this paper in 2021, and back then, transformers had just entered the computer vision research space through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community had been switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they were getting better and better performance. So in this work, we wanted to investigate whether truly convnets had lost their competitiveness, and whether it's possible to control all the design components to study whether convnets can be modernized to be on par with vision transformers at that time. We wanted to study whether the seeming performance gap between vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution, or due to other seemingly small design details. And we found the answer to be the latter. So after a lot of studying, of modernizing the design components of a convnet, we eventually got the model to be on par with very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that no matter whether you choose convnets or vision transformers, as long as you get everything correct, you'll get the same frontier-level performance on vision tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the importance of neural network architecture choice for making AI more useful?

items.answer:

I would say, as long as you get everything correct, as long as you explore the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. I think in the past many years, there haven't been innovations that have been widely adopted other than the mature architectures that we already were working with several years ago.

I do think, from a practical point of view, what data we train the model on matters more than the architecture choice. As long as the input/output interface stays the same, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The very basic function of neural networks or deep learning. As long as you get a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or other reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward layers at the right places, you'll be very close or at the frontier curve of this performance versus efficiency balance.

items.question: What evidence would you require before accepting that a neural network architecture change provides a real benefit?
items.object: Standards for demonstrating the benefits of neural network architecture changes
items.answer:
In an ideal world, we would have unlimited compute, right? First of all, I would require the benefit to be demonstrated on a state-of-the-art scale, not necessarily frontier models, but like 7B, 30B. I think scale is important for industry to really see the benefit, to be convinced about the change. But that's not always possible, so it's just in an ideal world.

If you want to study these mechanisms, architecture changes at smaller scales, like the ones we could do with reasonable resources, I would require first a hyperparameter sweep. We cannot demonstrate the new architecture just because it works on one set of hyperparameters better than the old model, especially when that hyperparameter is tuned just for that model. Ideally, each model should compare against each other on their own best hyperparameter settings. The most important hyperparameters would be learning rate, weight decay, optimizer types. It just bothers me a lot when people only tune the learning rate of their own method without tuning the learning rate of the baseline. That's kind of the easiest, most common fix for a lot of claims that turn out not to be generalizing.

Secondly, I would require the idea or the method to be demonstrated on more than one dataset, especially on reasonable-scale datasets. I would say ImageNet is still applicable today, but ideally they should also demonstrate the idea to work on some small-scale large language models, say, for example, training on FineWeb. But I understand that not every lab has the resources to do that. I'm a big fan of demonstrating ideas on a diverse range of datasets, at least the common datasets people work on. So I guess that's the two standards I would impose.

items.question: How do you assess whether internet-scale computer vision datasets are broad enough to support models that generalize to every task?
items.object: The breadth of internet-scale computer vision datasets
items.answer:
So I will first talk a little bit about the context. This paper is more vision-focused. Over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets, from more and more diverse sources. Initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then internet-scale datasets like DataCamp or Conceptual Captions, CC, from Google. They have seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger, from tens of thousands to billion scale. It was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from the internet. But in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are still nothing like each other.

We designed a very dumb experiment that doesn't make sense at all as a deep learning training program. Given three very large-scale computer vision datasets, we train a neural network to classify which dataset a particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem; it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. It's a multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, higher than 80% when you have three datasets. The random guessing accuracy would be 33%, but the model can be much better than that. So this means, to a model, these datasets are still very, very different. It has very clear cues to tell which dataset this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held-out validation sets. We are not predicting the training images.

But still, this has been surprisingly accurate, and that prompts us to reflect: have we really been successful in curating a large-scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in the computer vision domain? What kind of dataset is the end goal? It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criteria, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there.

A big story of the success of LM is that it's not a domain-specific model, right? We want the model to be able to do everything, and a common assumption is that we need the model to have seen everything during training. How much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we haven't reached that point yet, and it still makes sense to think about how we curate these datasets for the model to be really generalizing to every task we want the model to be good at.

items.question: How do you approach balancing different domains in a model's training data?
items.object: Balancing domains in a model's training data
items.answer:
I would say, yes, diversity of content, diversity of styles. I think a big lesson of deep learning is that if you want the model to be good at something, you better train it at something. And if you want to be good at everything, you need to train at everything. But in today's regime, we still have this trade-off problem, right? We don't have unlimited compute. Although we have built this giant data center, we still have limited compute, limited capacity of the model. So the different capabilities the model has learned may still compete with each other. Meaning that if you want the model to be better at coding, you might need to sacrifice a little bit on the model's, say, psychological counseling abilities for users, right? That's just an example. How do we develop a mixture of training data with enough representation for each thing we want the model to be good at, and to be good enough at? How to balance different domains of data is kind of an important design.

In our recent project of text-to-image generation, we actually found a surprisingly simple solution. It's not the best, but it's simple enough: divide all the domains you care about, roughly have the domains be of equal importance to each other. You don't want to have, say, how to do haircut equally represented as how to do coding, right? They are of different importance to most people. We want the model to train on much more data on coding rather than how to do haircut. But if you extend the concept of haircut to other daily life skills, at the appropriate level, if you control that to be about the same importance level as another domain, then you just collect high-quality data from each domain and mix them equally in your training data. That turns out to be good for a lot of our projects.

items.question: Why do you think language models drove such a broad jump in AI capabilities and adoption when computer vision had been around for much longer?
items.object: Language versus vision as a driver of advances in AI
items.answer:

Say if I take my current view, and it's just one image, one frame, the space it takes to store that image is much higher than the space to store the description of this image in language. The language could be stored in bytes, but the image would need to be stored in kilobytes. It's just a thousand times difference. So an image is worth actually more than a thousand words, right? It's really high throughput data, and we don't have enough compute to handle this data yet.

And also, with the current multimodal language models, we don't have a mechanism to let the model look back on the image to focus on specific areas, because everything is already encoded in the vision tokens. If the vision encoder is not good, the language model or the rest of the model can do nothing about it.

And language is on a much lower dimension space, where each word has a clear meaning. It's kind of the unsupervised learning by humans from nature. We prepare these words for the model in our human evolution process, that these concepts are important. And it's a very condensed concept. For example, a cup. To describe a cup from images, you need kind of thousands of images of cups. But just to describe a cup from language, you just need that one word. So the compute required to process that much information, that much detailed information, would naturally be much higher, and I don't think we are there yet.

items.question: Why do you see the multimodal language model failures examined in your study as a vision encoder problem?

items.answer: I think it's very much a vision encoder problem. These models only learn what they are taught to learn in training, right? If you don't impose the types of training task you want them to excel at, they will not be good during test time. So specifically in CLIP training, we are training image representations to be aligned with the caption representations. Usually, the captions focus more on the content of the image: what's out there, what objects are there, what are they doing? But less on explicitly the positions of these objects. If you have a human and dog in the image, the caption likely doesn't say whether the human is on the left or on the right. It just says human plays with dog. That's kind of the natural thing we want to say when we see such an image. And that's okay with humans. We don't usually care about who is on the left. But if you want a model to be answering these types of questions well, then we need to use that in training, and that's what current CLIP training doesn't care about. So we end up with a CLIP model that's going to be used as a vision encoder for multimodal language models, but it's not trained to be good at these spatial tasks or other types of tasks that we focus on in that study.
